items.title: Good Governance — Concept & Attributes
items.body:
## What is good governance?

**Governance** is the exercise of authority to manage a country's affairs; **good governance** is governance that is **citizen-centric, transparent and accountable**. The UN (UNESCAP) lists **eight attributes**.

| # | Attribute | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Participation | Citizens have a voice in decisions |
| 2 | Rule of law | Fair legal frameworks, impartially enforced |
| 3 | Transparency | Information is freely available and accessible |
| 4 | Responsiveness | Institutions serve stakeholders in reasonable time |
| 5 | Consensus-oriented | Mediates differing interests for broad agreement |
| 6 | Equity & inclusiveness | All feel they have a stake |
| 7 | Effectiveness & efficiency | Best use of resources |
| 8 | Accountability | Answerability of government, private sector, civil society |

## In the Indian context

- Reform motto: **'minimum government, maximum governance'**.
- **Good Governance Day** is observed on **25 December** (Atal Bihari Vajpayee's birth anniversary).
- Enablers of good governance in India: **RTI (transparency)**, **Citizen's Charters/Sevottam (responsiveness)**, **social audit (accountability)** and **e-governance (efficiency and access)**.
keyPoints: Good governance = citizen-centric, transparent and accountable administration.
UNESCAP's eight attributes: participation, rule of law, transparency, responsiveness, consensus-oriented, equity & inclusiveness, effectiveness & efficiency, accountability.
Indian reform motto: 'minimum government, maximum governance'.
Good Governance Day is 25 December (Vajpayee's birthday).
Key enablers: RTI, Citizen's Charter/Sevottam, social audit, e-governance.
items.mnemonic: 8 attributes → 'PART-CEEA': Participation, Accountability, Rule of law, Transparency; Consensus, Equity, Effectiveness, (responsivenes)... focus on the 4 core: Participation, Rule of law, Transparency, Accountability.

items.title: Right to Information (RTI) Act 2005
items.body:
## The transparency instrument

The **RTI Act 2005** (enacted 15 June 2005; in force **12 October 2005**) operationalises the right to know, flowing from **Article 19(1)(a)**. It replaced the never-enforced Freedom of Information Act 2002.

## Machinery & process

- Every public authority designates a **Public Information Officer (PIO)** who must reply within **30 days** (48 hours if life/liberty is at stake).
- **Appeal ladder:** PIO → **First Appellate Authority (FAA)** → second appeal to the **Central / State Information Commission (CIC/SIC)**.
- **Section 4** — proactive (suo motu) disclosure by public authorities to minimise applications.
- **Section 8** — exemptions (national security, sovereignty, cabinet papers, personal information with no public purpose), subject to a **public-interest override** (Sec 8(2)).

## RTI (Amendment) Act 2019

- Shifted the power to fix the **tenure, salaries and allowances** of the CIC/ICs (central and state) from the **Act itself** to **Central Government rules**.
- Earlier: fixed **5-year term** (or up to 65 years) with **salary parity to Election Commissioners**; critics said the change diluted the Commissions' independence.
keyPoints: RTI Act enacted 2005; came into force 12 October 2005; flows from Article 19(1)(a).
PIO must respond in 30 days (48 hours where life/liberty is involved).
Appeal ladder: PIO → First Appellate Authority → Information Commission (CIC/SIC).
Section 4 = proactive disclosure; Section 8 = exemptions with a larger-public-interest override.
RTI (Amendment) Act 2019 moved tenure/salary of Information Commissioners to Central Government rules.
items.mnemonic: RTI timeline '30/45' isn't right — remember 30 days for the PIO, 30 days for the first appeal, 48 hours for life & liberty.
items.source: RTI Act 2005 & RTI (Amendment) Act 2019, India Code (rti.gov.in)

items.title: Citizen's Charter & the Sevottam Model
items.body:
## Citizen's Charter

- A **Citizen's Charter** is a public document that sets out an organisation's **service standards, entitlements and grievance-redress channels**.
- Originated in the **UK in 1991** (John Major). India adopted it at the **1997 Conference of Chief Ministers** ('Action Plan for Effective and Responsive Government').
- **Six UK principles:** quality, choice, standards, value, accountability, transparency.
- It is **voluntary and non-justiciable** — a moral commitment, not a legally enforceable contract by itself.

## Sevottam ('Seva' + 'Uttam' = service excellence)

A DARPG framework to assess and improve public-service-delivery organisations, built on **three modules**:

| Module | Focus |
|---|---|
| 1. Citizen's Charter | Publish service standards |
| 2. Public grievance redress | Handle and resolve complaints |
| 3. Service delivery capability | Strengthen the organisation to deliver |

## From promise to entitlement

- **Public Service Delivery Guarantee laws** convert charter promises into **time-bound, penalty-backed** rights. **Madhya Pradesh (2010)** enacted India's first such law; Bihar (2011) and others followed.
keyPoints: Citizen's Charter originated in the UK (1991); India adopted it in 1997; it is voluntary/non-justiciable.
Six charter principles: quality, choice, standards, value, accountability, transparency.
Sevottam = Seva + Uttam; three modules: Citizen's Charter, grievance redress, service-delivery capability (DARPG).
Public Service Delivery Guarantee laws make service standards time-bound with penalties.
Madhya Pradesh enacted India's first Public Service Guarantee Act (2010).
items.mnemonic: Sevottam = 'Seva Uttam' → 3 C's: Charter, Complaints (redress), Capability.
items.source: DARPG Citizen's Charter & Sevottam guidelines (darpg.gov.in); MP Public Service Guarantee Act 2010

items.title: Social Audit & Accountability
items.body:
## What is social audit?

**Social audit** is a process in which **citizens and beneficiaries jointly verify official records** (muster rolls, bills, works) against the **actual work on the ground**, usually in a **Gram Sabha**. It is a frontline tool of **accountability and transparency**.

## Legal mandate

- **MGNREGA 2005, Section 17** makes it mandatory for the **Gram Sabha to conduct regular social audits** of all works under the scheme — the first large statutory social-audit mandate in India.
- Later extended in principle to other schemes and to social-audit units in states.

## Andhra Pradesh — the pioneer

- AP institutionalised independent social audits through the **Society for Social Audit, Accountability and Transparency (SSAAT)**.
- The AP model — independent audit teams, public reading of records in the Gram Sabha, and action on findings — became a **national reference** for social-audit standards.
keyPoints: Social audit = citizens/Gram Sabha verify official records against actual work on the ground.
MGNREGA 2005, Section 17 makes social audit by the Gram Sabha a statutory mandate.
It is a key accountability and anti-corruption tool in public expenditure.
Andhra Pradesh pioneered institutionalised social audits via SSAAT.
The AP model informed national social-audit standards and state social-audit units.

items.title: e-Governance — Types, NeGP & Digital India
items.body:
## e-Governance as administrative reform

**e-Governance** uses ICT to make government services **accessible, efficient, transparent and accountable**. Four interaction types:

| Type | Interaction | Example |
|---|---|---|
| G2C | Government → Citizen | Online certificates, pensions |
| G2B | Government → Business | MCA21 corporate filings, licences |
| G2G | Government → Government | Inter-agency data sharing |
| G2E | Government → Employee | Payroll, leave portals |

## National e-Governance Plan (NeGP) → e-Kranti

- **NeGP (approved 2006)** organised e-governance around **Mission Mode Projects (MMPs)** and aimed to deliver services through **common service-delivery outlets** ('...bring government services to the doorstep of the citizen').
- **e-Kranti (NeGP 2.0)** — approved 2015 as a **pillar of Digital India**; motto 'Transforming e-Governance for Transforming Governance'.
- **Digital India (launched 1 July 2015)** is the umbrella programme; from the governance angle it drives electronic service delivery and grievance redress.

## Grievance redress

- **CPGRAMS** (Centralised Public Grievance Redress and Monitoring System, DARPG) is the online portal for citizens to lodge and track complaints against public authorities.

> Note: the *technology* side of e-governance (India Stack, cyber security, DPDP Act) is covered under Science-Tech; here the focus is governance and service delivery.
keyPoints: e-Governance interaction types: G2C, G2B, G2G, G2E.
NeGP was approved in 2006 and built around Mission Mode Projects (MMPs).
e-Kranti (NeGP 2.0) is a pillar of Digital India — 'Transforming e-Governance for Transforming Governance'.
Digital India was launched on 1 July 2015 as the umbrella programme.
CPGRAMS (DARPG) is the centralised online public-grievance portal.
items.mnemonic: Four e-gov relationships all start with 'G2' → C, B, G, E (Citizen, Business, Government, Employee).
items.source: MeitY — NeGP / e-Kranti / Digital India (meity.gov.in); DARPG CPGRAMS

items.title: 2nd ARC & Andhra Pradesh's Governance Model
items.body:
## Second Administrative Reforms Commission (2nd ARC)

- Constituted in **2005**, first chaired by **M. Veerappa Moily** (later **V. Ramachandran**); submitted **15 reports**.
- Landmark reports for governance:
  - **1st — 'Right to Information: Master Key to Good Governance'**
  - **4th — 'Ethics in Governance'**
  - **11th — 'Promoting e-Governance: The SMART Way Forward'** (SMART = **S**imple, **M**oral, **A**ccountable, **R**esponsive, **T**ransparent)
  - **12th — 'Citizen Centric Administration: The Heart of Governance'**
- (The **1st ARC**, 1966, was chaired first by Morarji Desai, then K. Hanumanthaiah.)

## Andhra Pradesh — citizen-service delivery

| Initiative | What it does |
|---|---|
| **RTGS** (Real Time Governance Society) | Integrated command-and-control centre for real-time monitoring, data integration and grievance handling |
| **MeeSeva** ('at your service') | Single-window delivery of certificates and G2C services |
| **Mana Mitra** | Delivers a range of government services to citizens via **WhatsApp** (WhatsApp governance) |
| **e-Pragati** | State enterprise-architecture framework integrating departments |

- These illustrate the governance shift toward **paperless, doorstep and real-time** citizen service delivery.
keyPoints: 2nd ARC (2005) was first chaired by Veerappa Moily and submitted 15 reports.
1st report: 'RTI — Master Key to Good Governance'; 12th: 'Citizen Centric Administration'.
SMART governance = Simple, Moral, Accountable, Responsive, Transparent (11th report on e-Governance).
AP RTGS runs an integrated real-time monitoring and grievance command-and-control centre.
AP MeeSeva = single-window G2C service delivery; Mana Mitra delivers services via WhatsApp.
items.mnemonic: SMART = Simple, Moral, Accountable, Responsive, Transparent — the 2nd ARC's e-governance ideal.
items.source: Second ARC reports (arc.gov.in); AP Real Time Governance Society (rtgs.ap.gov.in)

items.title: Development processes — civil society, NGOs, SHGs, pressure groups & stakeholders
items.body:
## Actors in the development process

Development is no longer government-only; multiple **stakeholders** participate.

- **Civil society** — the space of voluntary, non-state, non-market associations (community groups, unions, faith and welfare bodies) that hold the state accountable and mobilise citizens.
- **NGOs (non-governmental organisations)** — organised non-profit bodies delivering services, advocacy and awareness (health, literacy, environment).
- **Self-Help Groups (SHGs)** — small (usually 10-20) voluntary groups, mostly of women, that pool savings and access bank credit for livelihoods; the backbone of India's community-driven poverty reduction.
- **Pressure groups** — organised interests (trade unions, farmer bodies, professional and business associations) that influence policy **without seeking political office**.
- **Stakeholders** — all who affect or are affected by a programme: citizens, PRIs, SHGs, NGOs, civil society, private sector and government.

## The Andhra Pradesh model (verified)

| Body | Role |
|---|---|
| **DWCRA** | Development of Women and Children in Rural Areas — early (1982-83) women's SHG scheme that seeded AP's SHG movement |
| **SERP** | Society for Elimination of Rural Poverty — runs **Velugu / Indira Kranthi Patham (IKP)**, federating lakhs of women's SHGs |
| **MEPMA** | Mission for Elimination of Poverty in Municipal Areas — the urban SHG counterpart |
| **DAY-NRLM** | National Rural Livelihoods Mission — the national SHG-federation programme AP feeds into |

AP's dense **women's self-help group** federations (SHG → Village Organisation → Mandal Samakhya) are among India's strongest, linking civil society to state anti-poverty delivery.
keyPoints: Development involves many stakeholders: civil society, NGOs, SHGs, pressure groups, PRIs, private sector, government.
Civil society = voluntary non-state, non-market associations that hold the state accountable.
A Self-Help Group (SHG) is a small (10-20) voluntary savings-and-credit group, mostly of women.
A pressure group (union, farmer/business body) influences policy without contesting elections.
AP: DWCRA (1982-83) seeded the SHG movement; SERP runs Velugu/Indira Kranthi Patham federating women’s SHGs; MEPMA is the urban arm.
SHG federation ladder: SHG → Village Organisation → Mandal Samakhya; feeds DAY-NRLM.
items.source: 2nd ARC (civil society/development); DAY-NRLM (rural.gov.in); AP SERP/Velugu-IKP & MEPMA (serp.ap.gov.in); DWCRA scheme

items.title: PYQ Precision — Aadhaar, Aspirational Districts & Platforms
items.body:
## Aadhaar Act 2016

- Passed as a **Money Bill** (Art 110); full name: Targeted Delivery of Financial and Other Subsidies, Benefits and Services Act.
- Purpose: targeted **DBT** of subsidies charged to the Consolidated Fund; **Section 57 struck down** (2018 Puttaswamy).

## Aspirational Districts Programme (2018)

- Anchored by **NITI Aayog**; ranks districts on **five themes**: health & nutrition, education, agriculture & water, financial inclusion & skilling, basic infrastructure.
- Motto: **Convergence, Collaboration, Competition**; extended as Aspirational **Blocks** Programme (2023).

## e-Governance platforms

| Platform | Function |
|---|---|
| **UMANG** | Unified mobile app for govt services |
| **DigiLocker** | Digital document storage |
| **MyGov** | Citizen engagement/participation |
| **CPGRAMS** | Public grievance redress |
| **CSCs** | Last-mile delivery outlets |
keyPoints: Aadhaar Act 2016 was passed as a Money Bill; enables targeted DBT of subsidies; Section 57 struck down (2018).
Aspirational Districts Programme (2018) is anchored by NITI Aayog with five themes.
UMANG = unified mobile app; DigiLocker = document storage; MyGov = citizen engagement.
CPGRAMS = grievance redress; CSCs = last-mile delivery, all under Digital India.
Aspirational Districts motto: Convergence, Collaboration, Competition.
items.source: UPSC 2017 Prelims; Aadhaar Act 2016; NITI Aayog; MeitY/DARPG

items.title: MPLADS, Department of Personnel & Urban Bodies
items.body:
**MPLAD Scheme:** funds are **non-lapsable** and carried forward, meant for **durable community assets**, with a share **earmarked for SC/ST areas** and **at least 10% of works inspected** at the district level.

**Administrative reform:** the **N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar Committee** urged personnel reform; the **Department of Personnel** was set up in **1970 under the Prime Minister**.

**Urban bodies:** the **National Institute of Urban Affairs (NIUA)** is the **apex body of the Ministry of Housing & Urban Affairs**; the **India Sanitation Coalition** is a platform that **mobilises funding for sustainable sanitation** (not a GoI+WHO body).
keyPoints: MPLADS funds are non-lapsable, for durable assets, with SC/ST earmarking and 10% district inspection.
The Department of Personnel was set up in 1970 under the PM; the N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar Committee had urged reform.
NIUA is the apex body of the Ministry of Housing & Urban Affairs; the India Sanitation Coalition mobilises sanitation funding.
